Session plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Teachers leave able to spot the difference between supporting an anxious student and helping them avoid, with a two-part phrase for the moment and a smaller-step move for the requests they hear most: postpone the test, skip the assignment, leave the room, check it one more time.

Materials

  • Index cards, one per teacher
  • The faculty quick reference (last slide), printed or linked
  • Board space for the avoidance loop

Flow

  1. 5 minOpening: the last request to get out of something (private cards)
  2. 5 minWhat anxiety wants, and the loop it runs on
  3. 7 minThe research on avoidance and accommodation
  4. 5 minSupport or accommodation?
  5. 5 minSay it in two parts (practice in pairs)
  6. 6 minSix requests, six smaller steps
  7. 4 minThree in-the-moment tools with research behind them
  8. 5 minThree students (small groups)
  9. 3 minOne phrase this week

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Thirty minutes: the opening card (3), what anxiety wants and the loop (5), the research (5), say it in two parts (5), six requests (6), three students with one card per group (4), one phrase this week (2). Share the faculty quick reference afterward.

Before you present
Two presenters, one voice.

A natural split: the counselor or psychologist presents what anxiety wants, the loop, and the accommodation research; learning support presents the requests, the smaller steps, and how they fit with learning plans.

Nobody here is doing it wrong.

Letting a scared student postpone a test is a kind thing to do, and most teachers have done it. Say so. The talk adds a second option, not a verdict on the first.

Be clear about learning plans.

Accommodations written into a student's learning plan stay exactly as written. This talk is about the extra, in-the-moment requests. Expect this question early and answer it plainly.

Keep real illness a yes.

A student who is sick goes to the nurse. The smaller-step moves are for the pattern of asking to leave right before the hard part.

Lynn Lyons, in her words.

Teachers may know her books or podcast. Present her framework (anxiety wants certainty and comfort, and avoidance feeds it) as hers, and the trial data as the research that backs it up.

Leave room for a teacher's own anxiety.

Some people in the room live with anxiety themselves or have an anxious child at home. Keep examples about students and keep the tone warm.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Anxiety looks different.

It can show up as stomachaches, anger, joking, perfectionism or a quiet student who never asks. Boys and students of color are often read as defiant when they're anxious. Name that early.

Real worries.

Some students are anxious about real things: money at home, a family member's immigration status, discrimination at school. A smaller step still helps in class, and the real problem goes to the counseling team.

Family views of worry.

Some families see anxiety as weakness or keep it private; others are anxious themselves and ask the school to remove every stressor. When talking with families, use the same two parts: the worry makes sense, and we're confident in your child.

Neurodivergent students.

For students with ADHD or autism, anxiety often overlaps with sensory overload or unclear instructions. Check the learning plan first; predictability helps everyone.

Language and presenting.

Students learning English may dread speaking in front of the class for reasons beyond anxiety. Offer the same smaller steps: present to you, then a small group.

LGBTQ+ students.

Locker rooms, partner choices and being called on by name can carry extra worry for LGBTQ+ students. Some avoidance is about safety, not anxiety. Ask privately before you treat it as an exposure step.

What the research says

Anxiety wants certainty and comfort. Avoiding the feared thing brings quick relief and teaches the worry the situation was dangerous, so it grows. The goal is to step into uncertainty and discomfort, a little at a time.

Lyons and Wilson, Anxious Kids, Anxious Parents, 2013; Wilson and Lyons, Playing with Anxiety, 2013

About 1 in 3 U.S. teens (31.9%) met criteria for an anxiety disorder at some point by age 18.

Merikangas et al., Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 2010

Nearly all parents of anxious children reported accommodating their child's anxiety, and more accommodation went with more severe anxiety.

Lebowitz et al., Depression and Anxiety, 2013

In a trial with 124 anxious children, a program that taught parents to cut back accommodation and use supportive statements worked as well as cognitive behavioral therapy given to the child.

Lebowitz et al., Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 2020 (SPACE)

In the largest trial of treatments for anxious children and teens, therapy built on gradual exposure helped 60%, medication 55%, both together 81%, and placebo 24%.

Walkup et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2008 (CAMS)

Anxious students who spent ten minutes writing about their worries right before an exam scored higher than those who didn't.

Ramirez and Beilock, Science, 2011

Students told that a racing heart can help performance scored higher on GRE math practice than students who weren't.

Jamieson et al., Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2010

Saying "I am excited" before a speech, a math test or singing improved performance over trying to calm down.

Brooks, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014
